title: Choosing a Career
summary: A career is an occupation in which opportunities for advancement or promotion are available over one's working life — a sequence of positions held during one's work-life, not a single job held for life. For example, an office assistant may become office superintendent and then office manager. The work done in the different positions is the career path, the way adopted for a career. Career planning means thinking carefully about the positive and negative aspects of possible careers and one's own interests, abilities, personality and skills before choosing.

The career chosen lays the foundation of one's life; it shapes life-style, values, attitudes and habits; in a competitive world the right choice at the start saves time and frustration; it helps a person discover and use his abilities; and it avoids aimlessly changing jobs. Choosing a career requires knowing one's interests, personality and skills.

Wage employment means serving another person for wages or salary, under a contract between employer and employee. The employer assigns the work and decides the terms and conditions; the employee works under supervision for a fixed income. Avenues: government offices, railways, banks, insurance companies, factories, trading firms, schools, colleges and hospitals — clerical jobs (office assistant, accounts clerk, bank clerk), technical jobs (after ITI or polytechnic training), laboratory assistants, telephone operators. Clerical jobs need skill in handling office machines (computers, photocopiers); telephone operators need fluency in language.

Self-employment is engaging in an economic activity of one's own and managing it oneself to earn a living. A person who starts a business and also employs others is self-employed. Areas: (1) small-scale retail business — grocery, stationery, cloth shops; (2) services based on skills — repair of cycles, scooters and watches, tailoring, hairdressing, beauty parlours; (3) professions — doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants, architects in private practice; (4) small-scale farming — dairy, poultry, fishery, horticulture, sericulture; (5) village and cottage industries — spinning, weaving, knitting; (6) arts and crafts — goldsmiths, blacksmiths, carpenters, potters. Clerical or technical jobs for others are wage employment, not self-employment.

Nature: self-employed — owner; wage-employed — employee. Position: own boss vs works under an employer. Earning: profit, no limit vs fixed wage or salary. Work: decided by oneself, varies vs specific and assigned by the employer. Risk: bears all risk vs none while employed. Freedom: free to decide vs bound by terms of employment. Self-employment is often preferred because one uses one's talents for one's own benefit, it is possible with little capital, one learns on the job, earnings are unlimited and it creates jobs for others and reduces unemployment.

Mental abilities (identifying opportunities, decision-making, dealing with customers, anticipating problems and bearing risk); alertness and foresight; self-confidence; knowledge of the business and technical skill; acquaintance with relevant laws (shop and establishment, tax, municipal and pollution rules); and personal qualities — honesty, sincerity, hard work, patience, good health. Dependence on others, laziness and mental imbalance are not qualities of a self-employed person.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (a) ________ employment means serving another person for wages or salary. (b) When a person engages in an economic activity and manages it on his own, it is known as ________.
Write True (T) or False (F): (a) There is no limit to earnings in wage employment. (b) Self-employment in business involves risk of loss borne by the owner.

(a) False — wages are fixed; earnings are unlimited in self-employment.
(b) True
Write True (T) or False (F): (a) A goldsmith cannot be self-employed as he must work under a jeweller. (b) Some capital is needed even to provide an individualised service for a price.

(a) False — a goldsmith can run his own workshop.
(b) True
vsa: Explain any two possible areas of self-employment with two examples each.

(1) Small-scale retail business — grocery store, stationery shop.
(2) Services based on skill — tailoring, cycle and scooter repair.
(Also professions, small farming, cottage industries, arts and crafts.)
What is meant by career? Give an example.

A career is an occupation that offers chances of advancement over one's working life — a sequence of positions held. Example: an office assistant who becomes office superintendent and then office manager.
State two reasons why self-employment is preferred to wage employment.

(1) One can use one's own talents and time for one's own benefit, with no limit on earnings.
(2) It can be started with little capital and one learns many things on the job; it also gives employment to others.
sa: Explain the difference between self-employment and wage employment.

Status: a self-employed person is his own boss; a wage-employed person works under an employer.
Earning: profit with no fixed limit vs a fixed wage or salary.
Risk and freedom: the self-employed bears all risk and decides freely; the employee bears no risk but must follow the employer's terms.
How does self-employment help reduce unemployment?

(1) The person employs himself instead of looking for a job.
(2) A growing self-employed business hires assistants and workers, creating more jobs.
(3) It promotes small and cottage industries in villages, giving local employment and reducing migration.

or: State three examples of self-employment based on professional qualifications.
A doctor running a private clinic; a lawyer practising in courts; a chartered accountant (or architect) with his own office.

sa: Explain the importance of choosing a career.

(1) It lays the foundation of one's working life and shapes life-style, values and habits.
(2) In a competitive world the right early choice saves time and avoids frustration and frequent job changes.
(3) It helps a person discover his abilities and use them, leading to satisfaction and progress.
State any three qualities required for success in self-employment.

(1) Self-confidence to take decisions and face problems.
(2) Alertness and foresight about market changes.
(3) Knowledge of the business and of relevant laws; also honesty and hard work.

or: State briefly the avenues of wage employment in business.

Clerical jobs (office assistant, accounts clerk) and technical jobs in government offices, railways, banks, insurance companies, factories, trading firms, schools and hospitals; after ITI or secretarial training, jobs as technicians, typists or computer operators.

sa: 'Self-employment is better than wage employment.' Discuss.

(1) One uses one's talents for one's own benefit and earnings are unlimited.
(2) It can be started with little capital.
(3) One is one's own boss with freedom of work, and learns on the job.
(4) It creates jobs for others. However, it involves risk, so it suits those with the right qualities.
la: Distinguish between self-employment and wage employment on the basis of nature, position, earning, risk bearing and freedom of work.

Nature: self-employment is engaging in one's own economic activity; wage employment is serving another for wages.
Position: the self-employed is the owner; the wage earner is an employee.
Earning: profit with no limit vs fixed wage or salary.
Risk bearing: the self-employed bears the risk of loss; the employee has no risk of reduced income while employed.
Freedom of work: the owner decides how to run the business; the employee must work as per the terms of employment.
Enlist any five areas of self-employment and give one example of each.

(1) Small-scale retail business — a grocery shop.
(2) Services based on individual skills — a tailoring or hair-dressing shop.
(3) Professions — a doctor's private clinic.
(4) Small-scale farming — dairy or poultry.
(5) Village and cottage industries — handloom weaving.
(6) Arts and crafts — goldsmith, carpenter, potter.
State any five qualities required for success in self-employment.

(1) Mental abilities — to identify opportunities, take decisions, deal with customers and bear risks.
(2) Alertness and foresight about changes in the market.
(3) Self-confidence.
(4) Knowledge of the business, including technical skill.
(5) Acquaintance with relevant laws.
(6) Honesty, sincerity, hard work and patience.
Explain any three possible areas of self-employment.

(1) Small-scale retail business — one person with one or two helpers can run a grocery, stationery or cloth shop.
(2) Services based on skills — repairing cycles, scooters and watches, tailoring, hairdressing.
(3) Professions — doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants and architects practising on their own.
(Also small-scale farming, cottage industries, arts and crafts.)
Give any six points of difference between self-employment and wage employment.

(1) Nature — own activity vs serving another.
(2) Position — owner vs employee.
(3) Earning — profit vs fixed wage.
(4) Work — self-decided and variable vs specific and assigned.
(5) Risk — borne by owner vs none.
(6) Freedom — free to decide vs bound by terms of employment.
(7) Capital — needed vs not needed.
